value.overview: The Sulphur-bellied Flycatcher is a medium-sized Neotropical tyrant flycatcher with a striking yellow belly, dark brown back, and bold rufous-and-dark wing and tail pattern. It breeds from Mexico south through Central America and parts of northern South America, then migrates to South America for the nonbreeding season. It is often heard before it is seen because of its loud, distinctive calls. The species commonly uses forest edges, clearings, plantations, and other partly open habitats.
value.classification: The Sulphur-bellied Flycatcher belongs to the family Tyrannidae, the largest family of primarily insect-eating passerine birds. Its scientific name is Myiodynastes luteiventris.
value.identification: Adults have a bright sulphur-yellow underparts, heavily streaked brown-and-white throat and upper breast, a dark brown crown and back, and rufous panels in the wings and tail. The head often shows a dark eye-line and contrasting pale supercilium. The bill is broad and slightly hooked, typical of an aerial insect-catching flycatcher. Its loud, emphatic calls are useful for identification, especially in dense woodland where the bird may remain concealed.
value.rangeHabitat: The Sulphur-bellied Flycatcher breeds from western and eastern Mexico through Central America to northern South America, including Colombia and Venezuela. It occurs in Costa Rica mainly as a seasonal migrant and passage bird, with records during both migration periods and some presence in the breeding season in suitable areas; it is not generally regarded as a common permanent resident throughout the country. In Costa Rica it uses humid and dry forest edges, second-growth woodland, plantations, gardens, and open areas with scattered large trees, often at low and middle elevations.
value.migrationStatus: The species is migratory. Birds breeding in Mexico and Central America, including those passing through or occurring seasonally in Costa Rica, generally move south to South America after the breeding season. Costa Rica is used chiefly as a migration and seasonal-use area, with occurrence varying by region, elevation, habitat, and time of year.
value.breeding: Breeding takes place mainly from spring into summer in the northern part of the range and during the corresponding wet-season period farther south. The species usually nests in natural tree cavities or abandoned woodpecker holes, although other enclosed sites may occasionally be used. The female lays a small clutch, and both adults defend the nesting area and feed the young. Nest placement and breeding timing vary across the broad geographic range.
value.dietFeeding: The Sulphur-bellied Flycatcher feeds mainly on large flying insects, including beetles, butterflies, moths, grasshoppers, and other arthropods. It commonly hunts from a conspicuous perch, making short sallies into the air or to vegetation before returning to the same or another perch. It may also take insects from foliage and occasionally consume small fruits or other available animal prey.
value.behavior: This flycatcher is often conspicuous because of its loud calls and habit of perching in exposed positions, but it can be difficult to observe in leafy forest edges. It is generally active during daylight and may defend feeding or nesting territories. Individuals frequently make short, direct flights to capture prey and may remain still for extended periods between foraging attempts. Vocal activity can increase during territorial and breeding periods.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not considered to be undergoing a sufficiently rapid decline to qualify for a threatened category, but detailed population monitoring is limited in parts of its range.
conservation.threats: Habitat loss and degradation may reduce breeding and stopover habitat, especially where mature trees, forest edges, and natural cavities are removed. Pesticide use and the loss of insect-rich vegetation may also reduce food availability locally.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect forest, woodland edges, mature trees, and natural nesting cavities in Costa Rica and throughout the species' range. Maintain pesticide-free native vegetation, support habitat-friendly farms and gardens, and report observations through structured bird-monitoring programs to improve knowledge of migration and population changes.
